one_liner: Parallel work-stealing Rust find(1) subset that lists a warm Linux kernel tree about 3.5x faster than GNU find.
what_it_does: minifind is a CLI that prints the paths under one or more directories. It filters them with ANDed find-style predicates: -name/-regex/-path/-lname, -type, -size, -mtime/-mmin families, -perm, -user/-group, -links, -inum, -newer, -readable, depth limits, --exclude pruning, -print0 and -quit/--max-results. It is a subset of find, not a drop-in: no -exec/-delete/-printf actions, no -o/-not/parentheses grammar, every PATH must be an existing directory, and by default it lists only d/f/l types and does not cross mount points. The crate also exposes minifind::run() so the pipeline can be driven from Rust.
how_it_is_fast: Most of the gap is parallelism: threads-1 walker threads (7 on the 8-thread test box) pull directory tasks from crossbeam-deque LIFO work-stealing queues. Each directory is read with raw getdents64 through rustix, and children are opened with openat relative to a shared parent fd. File type comes from d_type, so the default listing never stats an entry; metadata predicates statx lazily, after the name and type filters. Matches go to a dedicated output thread in 256-entry batches and through a 256 KB BufWriter; mimalloc is the global allocator.
when_to_use: Listing or name/type-filtering large local trees (source checkouts, build outputs, home directories) on a multi-core machine with a warm page cache, where a single-threaded find is the bottleneck
Scripts that need find-style metadata filters (-mtime, -size, -perm, -user, -newer) plus -print0 for xargs -0, without fd's gitignore and hidden-file rules
Background scans on busy Linux hosts: --idle puts workers in SCHED_IDLE and IOPRIO_CLASS_IDLE at nice +19 with 2 threads
I/O-throttled environments: -s/--max-scan-rate caps directories scanned per second
when_not_to_use: When you need find's actions or grammar (-exec, -delete, -printf, -o, -not, parentheses), file operands instead of directories, or find's deterministic depth-first output order; parallel workers emit in arbitrary order, so -quit/--max-results return an arbitrary match

When errors must be visible: by code reading, a directory that fails to open or read (EACCES, a getdents error) is skipped silently and the exit status stays 0. GNU find prints a diagnostic and exits 1

1-2 core hosts or cold caches: the README says the gap shrinks toward parity there, and no single-thread or cold-cache numbers are published. --threads accepts 2 to 65535, and AGENTS.md says more than 21 threads gives no gain
When total CPU time matters more than wall time: idle walkers poll with crossbeam Backoff::snooze (spin, then yield) instead of parking, and the benchmark reports wall time only
Windows: the std::fs fallback has no --one-filesystem (dev = 0) and reports device, pipe and socket entries as File

integration.form: CLI binary (cargo-dist installers, Homebrew tap); also a library crate exposing minifind::run()
integration.dependencies: mimalloc, crossbeam-channel/deque/utils, rustix, libc, globset, regex, governor, lexopt, signal-hook, normpath, itertools, anyhow
integration.platforms: Linux (getdents64 via rustix, statx, --idle), other Unix via rustix (stat instead of statx); Windows through a std::fs fallback. Release targets: x86_64 and aarch64 Linux (gnu, plus x86_64 musl), x86_64 and aarch64 macOS, x86_64 Windows
integration.thread_safety: CLI: n/a. Library run() spawns its own walker and output threads, installs process-wide signal handlers, and main() raises RLIMIT_NOFILE to the hard limit, so treat run() as one call per process
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: plain 'find DIR' and many single-dash spellings (-name, -type, -size, -newer, -print0, -xdev) work, but there are no actions or boolean operators. -o means --one-filesystem, not OR. Defaults differ (d/f/l only, no mount crossing), output order is nondeterministic, and unreadable directories are skipped silently with exit 0

gotchas: Harness flaw: benches/walk.rs runs each tool through Command::output() and discards the result. It checks neither the exit status nor that the two outputs match, so a failing or truncated run would still be timed. Only wall time is measured: 7 walker threads plus an output thread against single-threaded GNU find, with no CPU-time or per-thread figure.

By code reading: walk.rs returns early when open_child/open_root fails, and the for_each_entry result is discarded (let _ =). Unreadable or vanished directories therefore disappear from the output with no message, and the documented exit status stays 0. Output write errors are also ignored (unwrap_or(())).

The README numbers come from the 2026-06-19 'full-clock rerun' on the newly added fd-anchored walker. Later releases 0.9.0-0.10.2 added predicates, --idle and the man page without re-benchmarking. The GNU find version and build, and the rustc version, are not stated.

AGENTS.md still says ignore::WalkBuilder applies .gitignore filters by default. CLAUDE.md and Cargo.toml show ignore is now only a dev-dependency since the custom walker replaced it in 0.8.0, so trust the code over AGENTS.md.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick minifind over fd when you want find-style metadata predicates and no ignore-file filtering in a parallel walker. fd's catalogued win is over find -iregex/-iname matching, while minifind's is a plain listing, and no head-to-head between the two is published. Pick cligen/dents for a single-threaded Nim library hook, and dumac when you need du totals rather than paths.
verified_claims_summary: Criterion (100 samples, 80 s warm-up, 400 s measurement) on a 4-core/8-thread Xeon E5-1630 v3, warm page cache, over a shallow Linux kernel clone (100,871 entries, 6,201 directories). minifind defaults (fat-LTO release profile, mimalloc, 7 walkers) took 26.70 ms against 93.00 ms for the GNU find on PATH (version unstated), about 3.5x. Both runs included process startup and piped stdout into the harness; the harness checked neither output nor exit status.
status_note: Actively maintained (0.10.2, last commit 2026-10-10, MIT, 10 stars, AI-assisted development per CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) and easy to install as a binary. Treat it as a fast lister, not a find replacement: the speedup is mostly 8-thread parallelism, warm-cache only, and errors are swallowed silently (code reading, not run).
